column2: Hi there, today's question is on nominees' annuities.
Can they cut your inheritance tax, how do they work, and what's the catch?
I'm Steve Hunt.
I'm a Chartered Insurance Risk Manager and a Trust and Estate Practitioner,
and I've been in the industry since 1980,
and I'm here to answer the questions that you ask.
The short answer.
A nominees' annuity is a pension income for life, paid by an insurance company to
someone you choose after you die, such as a grown-up son or daughter.
Some insurers call it a non-dependent annuity.
In the UK, from 6 April 2027, a nominees' annuity bought together with your own
lifetime annuity is left out of the new inheritance tax charge on pensions.
Your son or daughter still pays income tax on it, unless you die before 75.
What is a nominees' annuity?
A nominees' annuity is an income for life that is paid to your nominee after you
die.
It is a pension death benefit, and it is paid by an insurance company.
Two words first.
An annuity is a deal with an insurance company.
You use pension money to buy a promise of a regular income, usually for life.
A nominee is a person you choose who is not your dependant.
Most often that is a grown-up son or daughter.
It could also be a grandchild, a brother, a sister or a friend.
The law that defines a nominees' annuity is the Finance Act 2004, Schedule 28,
paragraph 27AA.
That paragraph allows two ways of buying one.
The first way is to buy it together with your own lifetime annuity, while you are
alive.
The second way is for it to be bought after you die, with pension money that is left
over.
Both are called a nominees' annuity.
From April 2027, only the first way is left out of the new inheritance tax charge on
pensions.
That one difference is what this whole video is about.
Is a non-dependent annuity the same as a nominees' annuity?
Yes.
A non-dependent annuity is the name some insurers use for a nominees' annuity.
It is the same thing.
The name comes from who gets paid.
In pension law, your dependants are your husband, wife or civil partner, a child
under 23, or someone who depended on you for money.
That list is in the Finance Act 2004, Schedule 28, paragraph 15.
A nominee is someone who is not on that list.
So an annuity for a nominee is an annuity for a non-dependant.
What changes for pensions and inheritance tax on 6 April 2027?
From 6 April 2027, most unused pension money and most pension death benefits count
as part of your estate for inheritance tax.
Your estate is everything you own when you die.
The change comes from the Finance Act 2026.
Section 66 puts a new section 150A into the Inheritance Tax Act 1984.
Section 71 says the change applies to deaths on or after 6 April 2027.
It is the date of death that counts.
If your estate is big enough to pay inheritance tax, the rate on the taxable part is
Inheritance tax is the same across the UK.
Then income tax can follow.
If you die aged 75 or over, your son or daughter pays income tax on the pension
money they receive, at their own rate.
That is the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003, section 579A.
So the same pension money can be taxed twice.
First inheritance tax, then income tax.
That does not mean every pension pays 40% inheritance tax.
Allowances, exemptions and your age when you die all matter.
And where your son or daughter pays the inheritance tax on a pension themselves, the
law gives them a deduction, so the same tax is not counted again as income.
That is section 567B of the 2003 Act, added by the Finance Act 2026, section 70.
Is a nominees' annuity free of inheritance tax from April 2027?
A nominees' annuity bought together with your own lifetime annuity is left out of
the new pension inheritance tax charge when you die.
A nominees' annuity bought any other way is not.
The new section 150A of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 has a list of benefits that are
left out.
Section 150A, subsection 6, paragraph c, lists, and I quote, a dependants' annuity,
or a nominees' annuity, that was purchased together with a lifetime annuity payable
to the member.
In plain words, if you buy your own lifetime annuity, and at the same time you buy a
nominees' annuity for your son or daughter, the nominees' annuity is not added to
the pension inheritance tax sum when you die.
The exclusion is narrow.
If a nominees' annuity is bought after you die, with your leftover pension money, it
does not get this exclusion.
The leftover pension money counts towards your estate first.
What does bought together mean?
Bought together means the nominees' annuity is linked to your own lifetime annuity
when you buy it.
It cannot be added years later.
The pension tax rules say how the two can be linked.
They can be one joint life annuity.
Or they can be two separate annuities, bought no more than seven days apart.
That is the Finance Act 2004, section 278B.
So the nominees' annuity has to be arranged at the start, when you buy your own
annuity.
Does my son or daughter pay income tax on a nominees' annuity?
It depends on your age when you die.
If you die aged 75 or over, your son or daughter pays income tax on each payment, at
their own rate, as the payments arrive.
If you die before 75, the payments can be free of income tax.
For deaths at 75 or over, the rules are in the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions)
Act 2003, sections 579A and 579D.
The tax is paid year by year, spread over the rest of their life.
It is not all taxed in one go.
For deaths before 75, the rule for a nominees' annuity bought together with your own
annuity is section 646B, subsection 3, of the same Act.
There are conditions, but the income can be tax free.
So being left out of inheritance tax does not always mean free of income tax.
They are two different taxes, with two different sets of rules.
What do the numbers look like?
Here is a worked example.
Mr Miggins is made up.
The tax rates in his story are real.
Mr Miggins is 80.
He is a widower.
His estate is already well over his inheritance tax allowances.
He wants to leave £100,000 of pension money to his daughter, Amy.
Amy pays income tax at 40% on all of it.
He dies after 6 April 2027, with the £100,000 still in his pension pot.
First, inheritance tax.
That leaves £60,000.
Then income tax.
Mr Miggins was over 75, so Amy pays income tax on the £60,000 she takes out.
At 40%, that is £24,000.
Amy is left with about £36,000 from the £100,000.
That is the double tax at work.
Now say Mr Miggins had used that £100,000 years earlier, at the same time as he
bought his own lifetime annuity, and bought a nominees' annuity for Amy as part of
it.
When he dies, there is no pension pot left to tax.
The nominees' annuity is left out of the pension inheritance tax sum.
Amy's income starts, and she pays income tax on each payment as it arrives, at her
own rate.
How much income Amy gets depends on the insurer's terms on the day the annuity is
bought.
Income tax rates in Scotland are different.
What are the catches?
There are six catches to know about.
First, timing.
The nominees' annuity has to be bought together with your own lifetime annuity.
You cannot add one later.
Second, it is for keeps.
Once the cooling off period has passed, an annuity usually cannot be changed,
cancelled or cashed in.
If your family or your plans change, the annuity stays as it is.
Third, your own income is lower.
Part of your pension money pays for your son or daughter's future income, so less is
left to pay you.
Fourth, if your son or daughter dies before you, the nominee's part usually just
stops.
That depends on the contract.
Fifth, not every annuity provider offers a nominees' annuity.
Some insurers also set a minimum age for the nominee.
Sixth, there is an open legal question about gifts.
Is buying a nominees' annuity a gift for inheritance tax?
There is no definitive legal answer yet.
The exclusion in section 150A deals with what happens when you die.
It does not settle whether buying the nominees' annuity in the first place was a
gift.
Under the Inheritance Tax Act 1984, section 3, subsection 1, a gift for inheritance
tax is called a transfer of value.
It is anything that makes your estate worth less.
Two other sections matter.
Section 10 says a deal is not a transfer of value if you did not mean to give anyone
a free benefit, and the deal was at arm's length.
Section 12, subsection 2ZA, protects pension rights that are not used.
In 2020 the Supreme Court decided a pension inheritance tax case, HMRC v Parry.
That case was about moving a pension and not taking benefits.
It did not decide whether buying a nominees' annuity is a gift.
If buying one were treated as a gift to your son or daughter, the usual seven year
rule for gifts would apply.
That is section 3A of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984.
Some families cover that seven year risk with life cover written in trust, such as a
whole of life plan.
What are the three questions to keep apart?
There are three separate questions.
One.
Is the nominees' annuity counted for inheritance tax when you die?
For one bought together with your own lifetime annuity, the law says no, from 6
April 2027.
Two.
Does your son or daughter pay income tax on it?
Yes, if you die at 75 or over.
It can be tax free if you die before 75.
Three.
Was buying it a gift?
The law has not settled that yet.
To sum up.
A nominees' annuity, also called a non-dependent annuity, is an income for life paid
to someone you choose after you die.
Bought together with your own lifetime annuity, it is left out of the new pension
inheritance tax charge from 6 April 2027.
It has to be set up at the start, it usually cannot be undone, and not every
provider offers one.
Tax rules can change, and how they apply depends on your own circumstances.
